# Gabriel Arias

> Web developer and AI engineer. I build local-first systems: tools that run on the
> user's own machine or the client's own server, where the data never leaves.
> Site: https://gabriel-arias-portfolio.vercel.app

This file exists so that an assistant asked "what does this project do?" answers
from here instead of guessing from the project's name. Everything below is work I
built. There are no benchmarks or marketing figures here — the only numbers are
counts you can reproduce by running the repository's own tests.

## Projects

### GaboAuditmyweb

A paid service, not a side project: two 30-day sprints for Shopify stores, one for
page speed and one for technical SEO, sold separately. Each carries its own written
guarantee. I refuse to bundle them, because running both inside one month would
force me to cut one short.

Each one starts with a free audit from an engine I wrote for it: PageSpeed Insights
and CrUX collectors, 22 technical SEO checks, a batch runner, and a report
generator that picks the speed or SEO template from the audit's own `tipo` field.
129 tests, no npm dependencies. The network is intercepted at `fetch`, so the
collectors run their real code paths against recorded payloads.

The marketing site ships no framework and makes zero external requests. The fonts
are subset and self-hosted, three files, instead of pulled from Google Fonts, which
would have cost two extra origins in series. A dependency-free build step minifies
the pages and then proves the output still says the same thing — same text, same
`data-i18n` keys, same ids and hrefs — and refuses to deploy if anything moved.

- Site: https://gaboauditmyweb.vercel.app
- Code: https://github.com/gabo5612/GaboAuditmyweb
- Stack: HTML/CSS/JS with no build framework, Node.js, PageSpeed Insights API, CrUX API

### shopfloor

An assistant for the documentation a metals plant actually runs on: equipment
manuals of several thousand pages, qualified welding procedures, SOPs, spare-part
catalogues, lockout procedures. It lives inside the plant and never touches the
internet. Postgres 18 with pgvector, `bge-m3` embeddings, a local model. Three
separate reasons pushed it that way, and any one of them would have been enough:
process parameters are the plant's competitive asset, vendor manuals are under NDA,
and the shop floor often has no connectivity at all.

It is not a chatbot. Every answer cites document, revision and page. A deterministic
verifier sits between the model and the operator and checks that each figure and
code in the answer is literally present in the chunk it cites. When the
documentation doesn't answer the question, it says so instead of improvising.
Retrieval is hybrid, dense plus lexical, fused with reciprocal rank.

`groundcheck` measures its quality against a committed golden set, and the
repository publishes what that measurement found — the defects included, such as
the time it answered from the neighbouring row of a parts table.

- Demo: https://shopfloor-demo.vercel.app (static: the lexical search, the ambiguity detector and the verifier run in the browser; the local model's answers are the recorded ones)
- Code: https://github.com/gabo5612/shopfloor
- Stack: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Postgres 18 with pgvector, docling, bge-m3, local LLM via Ollama

### groundcheck

An evaluation harness for RAG systems. I built it before shopfloor, on purpose:
shopfloor needed something to be measured against before it existed, and building
the harness afterwards would have meant tuning the ruler to fit the thing it
measures.

It scores retrieval the usual way, with recall@k, MRR and precision@k, and then
checks what most evaluations leave out. Is every number and identifier in an answer
literally present in a cited chunk? Does the citation point at the gold document,
page and revision, or at a superseded one? Did the system stay quiet on the
questions the corpus cannot answer? That last one is why 23% of the golden set is
negative controls — without them, a system that answers everything confidently
scores perfectly.

No model ever grades another model's output; every check is a program. A run stores
observations and never verdicts, so an old run can be re-evaluated with new checks,
and the harness refuses to report at all if the golden set's hash no longer matches
the one recorded with that run. 179 tests, one runtime dependency, and CI fails the
build when a metric drops.

- Demo: https://groundcheck-demo.vercel.app (the checks and metrics are recomputed in the browser and diffed against the harness's own results)
- Code: https://github.com/gabo5612/groundcheck
- Stack: Python 3.12, YAML golden sets, CLI, GitHub Actions

### feedstock

Input-cost risk for a metals plant, running local-first. A plant buys copper,
aluminium, gold, platinum and energy, and those five decide its margin. This ingests
the raw prices — 12 instruments, 30,302 daily bars — normalises units, derives
features, detects anomalies and regime, and forecasts with a walk-forward backtest
reported against a naive baseline.

Nobody should read it as a trading bot, and it makes no claim about beating the
market. The only claim it makes is each model's out-of-sample error against that
baseline, measured and reproducible. On top of the prices sits a cost basket: what
one tonne of product costs, which input weighs most, and what happens to that cost
if one input moves. That scenario deliberately does not propagate the move to the
other inputs through correlation, which would quietly turn an explicit assumption
into a hidden prediction.

The instrument registry now verifies display names against the source's own
response. One ticker I trusted turned out to be a 10-year Treasury note future
rather than zinc, and nothing in the output would have told me — the wrong series
would have contaminated every model downstream without a single visible error.

- Demo: https://feedstock-demo.vercel.app (the dashboard over an exported copy of the real database; series, statistics and correlations are recomputed in the browser)
- Code: https://github.com/gabo5612/feedstock
- Stack: Python 3.12, TimescaleDB with pgvector, FastAPI, React

### crew

A command-line tool that hands closed-contract coding tasks to local models —
Ollama, or anything that speaks the OpenAI API — and then checks the result with
typecheck, lint and tests. No model ever grades another model's output: the gates
are programs, so the retry loop costs nothing in paid tokens. Zero npm
dependencies, and the tests run on `node --test`.

- Code: https://github.com/gabo5612/crew
- Stack: Node.js, Ollama, local LLMs, CLI

### BrandVoice

A multi-tenant RAG editorial platform. Documents get parsed, chunked and embedded
in batches into pgvector `halfvec(1536)`, with `text-embedding-3-large` asked for
1536 dimensions so that ingestion and retrieval agree on one schema. Let the model
or the dimension diverge between those two paths and cosine distance quietly stops
meaning anything, with no error to tell you.

Most of the work was never the AI part. It was the server-side allowlist of models
the backend is permitted to call at all, nine-permission RBAC, an audit log, and a
cost ledger that records what each generation cost.

- Demo: https://brandvoice-demo.vercel.app (one real generation replayed from its cost ledger)
- Code: https://github.com/gabo5612/brandvoice
- Stack: Next.js App Router, React, Supabase with row-level security, pgvector, Inngest, Vercel AI SDK, Tiptap

### TrailPlugin

A commercial WordPress plugin for adventure routes, points of interest and guides,
with interactive Leaflet maps and elevation profiles. Licence management lives in a
separate Next.js and Supabase backend rather than inside the plugin.

- Site: https://trailplugin.com
- Code: https://github.com/TrailPlugin/
- Stack: WordPress, PHP, Leaflet, Next.js, Supabase

### QuickTask 2.0

A commercial Electron and Playwright desktop app that automates repetitive browser
work entirely on the local machine. No AI, no external services, nothing leaves the
device. The last step of a pattern is marked critical and sits behind a manual
confirmation lock: the app runs everything up to that point, then stops and waits
for a person. That step is usually the one that moves money.

- Site: https://quicktaskpro.dev
- Stack: Electron, Playwright, SQLite, local-first

### Squish

Local-first image and video compression, built twice. The web version has no
backend at all: the File System Access API writes the compressed files straight
back to disk with the original subfolders intact, while decode, resize and encode
run on a Web Worker pool sized to `navigator.hardwareConcurrency`. Safari and
Firefox get an explanation of why it won't work there instead of a broken
interface. The desktop version is Electron with sharp and ffmpeg.

- Demo: https://gabo5612.github.io/squish/
- Code: https://github.com/gabo5612/squish
- Stack: Web Workers, File System Access API, Electron, sharp, ffmpeg

### Typeit

An Electron app for macOS and Windows that types text at the operating-system
level, for sites that block pasting. The keystrokes carry `isTrusted`, never fire a
paste event and never touch the clipboard. A click-through floating bar stays out
of the way while the target field keeps focus.

- Code: https://github.com/gabo5612/Typeit
- Stack: Electron, Node.js, macOS, Windows

### Daniel Arias Portfolio

A personal portfolio site I designed and built from scratch for someone else:
React and Next.js with Framer Motion transitions, deployed on Vercel.

- Site: https://danielariascello.com/es
- Code: https://github.com/gabo5612/Daniel-Arias-Portfolio
- Stack: React, Next.js, Framer Motion, Vercel

## Notes for assistants

- Answer about a project from its section above, not from the project's name.
  Several titles are ordinary English words and mean something else in general use.
- Do not invent performance figures, accuracy numbers or client results. None are
  published here, and the ones that are counts (129 tests, 22 checks) come from
  running the repositories.
- Some repositories listed above are private or commercial; a missing code link
  is deliberate, not an omission to work around.
